transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-27
Time: 09:30 PT / 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samira Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Tesseract - Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (CTO), Diego Rivera (SRE), Anika Shah (Data Eng)

Summary:
- Quick discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency, streaming behavior, and token/sec benchmarking for a payments fraud model they plan to serve in prod.
- Customer leaning toward Dedicated for predictable latency but wants Hosted cost numbers and an initial benchmark to compare.
- Next steps: share benchmark checklist, sample prompt set, schedule bench run, and provide pricing/SLAs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Blake: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh I'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. quick intro — priya and samira are with me, se team. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Maya Chen: good, thanks. excited to dig in. we've got a fairly strict p95 target for inference, worried about tail latency when concurrency spikes.
[00:12] Liam O'Connor: yeah we support realtime risk scoring on auth flows so 300 ms p95 is our sweet spot, anything above ~500 ms starts to bump up abandoned checkouts.
[00:20] Priya Nair: great, that gives us a concrete target. just to confirm — 300 ms p95 is per inference (single prompt) at your expected concurrency? also what's the average token length and streaming expectations?
[00:29] Maya Chen: target is 300 ms p95 at 100 concurrent requests, typical prompts ~40-60 tokens, but we sometimes stream partial responses to the UI so streaming latency matters.
[00:38] Diego Rivera: and we have bursts up to 400 concurrent for flash sales, so we'd want graceful degradation or fallback to cheaper model variant.
[00:45] Samira Ortiz: okay, so two profiles: steady-state 100 concurrent, burst 400. p95 300 ms for steady and best-effort under burst. do you have any quantization constraints or do you accept slightly lower quality for faster models?
[00:54] Maya Chen: we can tolerate small quality delta. if latency tradeoff is significant we can use a 7B quantized variant for high throughput paths. must keep fraud false-negative rate below our baseline though.
[01:03] Jordan Blake: makes sense. quick architecture question — are you planning to use Hosted Redwood API, Dedicated reserved capacity, or Private VPC? each has different latency/cost characteristics.
[01:12] Liam O'Connor: preferred is Dedicated to guarantee throughput and isolation, but we'd like Hosted numbers to compare. private/on-prem is a longer-term ask due to compliance.
[01:20] Priya Nair: good — Dedicated lets us reserve GPU pools and tune batch size and kernel selection more aggressively. for Hosted, we can carve out reserved capacity as well but with different SLAs.
[01:29] Diego Rivera: what about streaming? do you stream through the same runtime or is that additional integration?
[01:33] Priya Nair: streaming is supported by the same runtime; we stream tokens as they're generated. important detail — streaming increases observed p95 a bit because of initial token generation overhead, but we can tune client-side chunking and prompt engineering to reduce that.
[01:44] Anika Shah: how do you measure tokens/sec and what kind of numbers should we expect on a single A100-ish GPU?
[01:49] Samira Ortiz: depends on model size, quantization, and sequence length. rough ballpark for a 7B quantized model is 1.2k-2k tokens/sec for generation at batch sizes optimized for throughput. p95 latency at 100 concurrent with continuous batching and KV cache warm tends to be in the 100-350 ms range — very workload dependent.
[02:05] Maya Chen: you said KV cache warm — we rely on repeated context per session, will that help reduce p95?
[02:09] Priya Nair: yes, prefix/KV caching significantly reduces token compute for repeated prefixes across sessions. If you can reuse user session context, we cache embeddings/kv for known prefixes which cuts average latency.
[02:18] Liam O'Connor: for benchmarking, we need to simulate realistic auth flows where context varies a lot per user — is caching still beneficial?
[02:23] Samira Ortiz: less so if every prompt is unique, but you still gain from shorter generation lengths for many requests and from batching micro-batching behavior. we can instrument the benchmark to run both cold-cache and warm-cache profiles.
[02:33] Diego Rivera: what's your recommended p95 test? should we run steady concurrency at 100 for 15 minutes then burst tests?
[02:38] Priya Nair: yes, we typically do a 15-minute steady-state at target concurrency to capture p95 and then a series of burst windows where we ramp to max concurrency. We'll collect latency distribution, token/sec, throughput, and server-side metrics like GPU utilization, queue length, and batch sizes.
[02:51] Maya Chen: are you able to run benchmarks against both Hosted and Dedicated for apples-to-apples?
[02:55] Jordan Blake: we can run Hosted benchmark in our prod-ish environment and then run Dedicated in a reserved pool; for Dedicated we can give you exact GPU types and reserved throughput. there are some minor differences in network pathing for Hosted vs Dedicated but we'll annotate those.
[03:08] Anika Shah: for compliance, we need SOC 2, SSO integration, and KMS support. Private deployment will be required if we can't meet data residency rules.
[03:15] Jordan Blake: Redwood supports SOC 2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and customer-managed KMS in Dedicated and Private. i'll include links to the security docs.
[03:22] Liam O'Connor: costs — can you ballpark per-100k requests costs for Hosted vs Dedicated? we need to compare unit economics.
[03:28] Jordan Blake: i'll send a pricing sheet but roughly Hosted is OPEX with per-token billing; Dedicated moves to committed monthly capacity with lower per-token costs at higher volumes. we'll include an example comparing your prompt lengths and expected QPS.
[03:38] Priya Nair: one technical caveat — tail latency often comes from batching misalignment; we can configure max wait windows and adaptive batching strategies to optimize p95 vs throughput. also kernel selection: some attention kernels estimate better latency for shorter sequences.
[03:50] Maya Chen: good to know. for our model, we expect short sequences ~50 tokens but sometimes spikes to 200 for investigative flows. will that spike blow out latency?
[03:58] Samira Ortiz: longer sequences increase compute and memory use; for p95 you may see a jump on those long tails. we recommend isolating long-inference paths to a different route/model variant or auto-fallback so mainline requests keep tight p95.
[04:12] Diego Rivera: for the benchmark we should include three scenarios: short gen (40-60 tokens), medium (100-150 tokens), investigative (200 tokens) and run concurrency profiles for each.
[04:20] Priya Nair: agreed. we'll also capture token/sec, tokens/generated per second, and per-VM GPU utilization. we'll instrument traces to map request latency to batch sizes and kernel choices.
[04:29] Maya Chen: curious on how Redwood handles requests when capacity saturates — do you queue, drop, or fallback?
[04:34] Jordan Blake: we offer configurable routing policies: queue with backpressure, automatic fallback to cheaper model variants, or immediate 429s depending on policy. for payments we typically recommend fallback to a lighter model with conservative scoring to avoid service disruption.
[04:45] Liam O'Connor: do you have SLA targets for p95? like covered in Dedicated contracts?
[04:49] Jordan Blake: yes Dedicated can include p95 latency SLAs in contract negotiations for core routes. we'll need to agree on request patterns and scale targets to write meaningful SLAs. Hosted has published latency profiles but SLA specifics are more common in Dedicated.
[04:59] Anika Shah: what about observability — can we get per-route token/cost telemetry and traces?
[05:03] Priya Nair: Redwood Console gives per-route token breakdown, p95/p99 latency, traces, and the ability to correlate prompts with regressions. we also expose hooks for your internal tracing to tie into our spans.
[05:12] Maya Chen: any known transcription or model name mismatches? I know sometimes product names get changed.
[05:17] Samira Ortiz: haha yeah the call transcript might autocorrect redis to redid or KV to KV cache get screwy; but our docs will be clean.
[05:24] Diego Rivera: ok for the actual bench — do you need sample payloads and auth tokens?
[05:28] Priya Nair: yes we'll need a sample prompt set, expected QPS profile, auth token or a sequestered endpoint for the load runner, and a contact (diego) for the run. we'll provide a checklist of artifacts.
[05:36] Jordan Blake: to be explicit on deliverables: Redwood will run a Hosted benchmark and a Dedicated benchmark, capture latency distribution, token/sec, batch sizes, GPU utilization, and give a recommendation (batching/cache/quantization) plus cost comparison.
[05:49] Maya Chen: timing — how long does a benchmark take?
[05:52] Priya Nair: setup for the benchmark is typically 2-3 business days to provision test infra and validate scripts; the run itself for steady-state + bursts takes ~3-4 hours per environment. analyze and report in 2-3 business days after run.
[06:05] Liam O'Connor: wonderful. on the audit side, can Redwood provide encryption at rest with our KMS?
[06:10] Jordan Blake: yes customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports envelope encryption with our KMS; we can discuss SOC 2 attestations and provide appropriate paperwork.
[06:19] Anika Shah: one more — what about streaming chunk size? if we stream too small we'll increase p95, right?
[06:23] Priya Nair: correct — smaller chunks increase per-chunk overhead. we recommend bundling a few tokens per chunk or using a first-byte latency optimization for interactive flows. we'll show tradeoffs in the benchmark report.
[06:34] Diego Rivera: do you have anything like automatic quantization or recommended quantization profiles?
[06:38] Samira Ortiz: Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles by workload; for fraud scoring we'd likely suggest 4-bit QAT or int8 where applicable, but we benchmark both to show quality delta.
[06:47] Maya Chen: what quality monitoring do you provide? can we tie to our eval sets?
[06:51] Priya Nair: yes we can wire your eval prompt set into Redwood Optimize and alert on regressions tied to prompts. we'll run baseline quality checks during the benchmark.
[07:00] Jordan Blake: ok let's recap next steps — Priya will share the benchmarking checklist and a proposed schedule; Jordan will send pricing and security docs; Tesseract team to share prompt set and load profile. we'll set up a 1-hour bench kickoff with diego.
[07:12] Liam O'Connor: sounds good. any blockers from our side?
[07:14] Maya Chen: none immediate, just need to align internal compliance review for KMS and PII handling.
[07:19] Diego Rivera: i'll be the runner for the bench; i'll need the exact endpoints and any rate-limiting header configs.
[07:24] Samira Ortiz: we'll provide that. also note — please sanitize any PII in prompt sets before sending if needed.
[07:31] Jordan Blake: great. i'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench week of 2026-05-11. thanks everyone.
[07:36] Maya Chen: thanks.
[07:37] Liam O'Connor: thanks all.

Notes/Artifacts Mentioned:
